title: John Hammond's theater scheme and the band's walkout
summary: After Connie's Inn, Hammond's idea of opening a theater failed when half the outspoken band showed up, because they disliked Hammond; Procope laments the TV tribute and Hammond's Goodman devotion.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: When Fletcher's -- well, this is the only time, when we left Connie's Inn, and we were, you know, sort of knocking around, and then John Hammond came up with this idea of getting this theater down on 12th Street someplace, and he opened this theater, and then he had -- well, I guess on the surface it was a good idea. Fletcher, you know, advertised, 'Opening in this theater,' and of course he was very disliked by the men in Fletcher's band, and the men in Fletcher's band were very outspoken, very independent. You know, they weren't just lackey dogs in a way of speaking. So on the opening day of the theater, about half the band showed up, and it never got off the ground.
Just because they disliked John Hammond.
And as you say, that's very true. And I sat -- I sat home a few weeks back and they had a tribute to John Hammond on channel, what is it, 13?
And I said, 'Now, that's a damned shame.'
Yeah, and all these people he did so much for, you know, and he had this band, Benny Goodman. Benny Goodman, who was his alter-ego, his hero.
Yeah, his brother-in-law. Yeah. Everything is the great King of Swing, which is a whole new story and a whole new something else, yeah. The King of Swing.
